{{short description|Function used as a performance test problem for optimization algorithms}}
[[Image:Rosenbrock-contour.svg|thumb|right|300 px|Plot of the Rosenbrock function of two variables. Here <math>a=1, b=100</math>, and the minimum value of zero is at <math>(1,1)</math>.]]
In [[mathematical optimization]], the '''Rosenbrock function''' is a non-[[convex function|convex]] [[function (mathematics)|function]], introduced by [[Howard Harry Rosenbrock|Howard H. Rosenbrock]] in 1960, which is used as a [[Test functions for optimization|performance test problem]] for optimization [[algorithm]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Rosenbrock|first=H.H.|title=An automatic method for finding the greatest or least value of a function|journal=The Computer Journal|year=1960|volume=3|issue=3|pages=175–184|doi=10.1093/comjnl/3.3.175| issn=0010-4620 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It is also known as '''Rosenbrock's valley''' or '''Rosenbrock's banana function'''.

The [[global minimum]] is inside a long, narrow, [[parabola|parabolic]]-shaped flat valley. To find the valley is trivial. To converge to the global minimum, however, is difficult.

The function is defined by

:<math>f(x,y) = (a-x)^2 + b(y-x^2)^2</math>

It has a global minimum at <math>(x,y)=(a,a^2)</math>, where <math>f(x,y)=0</math>. Usually, these parameters are set such that <math>a = 1</math> and <math>b = 100</math>. Only in the trivial case where <math>a=0</math> the function is symmetric and the minimum is at the origin.

==Multidimensional generalizations==

Two variants are commonly encountered.

[[File:Rosenbrock3.gif|thumb|300px|Animation of Rosenbrock's function of three variables.<ref>{{cite book|last=Simionescu|first=P.A.|title=Computer Aided Graphing and Simulation Tools for AutoCAD users|year=2014|publisher=CRC Press|location=Boca Raton, FL|isbn=978-1-4822-5290-3|edition=1st}}</ref>]]

One is the sum of <math>N/2</math> uncoupled 2D Rosenbrock problems, and is defined only for [[parity (mathematics)|even]] <math>N</math>s:
: <math>f(\mathbf{x}) = f(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N) = \sum_{i=1}^{N/2} \left[100(x_{2i-1}^2 - x_{2i})^2
+ (x_{2i-1} - 1)^2 \right].</math><ref>{{cite journal |first=L. C. W. |last=Dixon |first2=D. J. |last2=Mills |title=Effect of Rounding Errors on the Variable Metric Method |journal=Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications |volume=80 |pages=175–179 |year=1994 |url=http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=179711 |doi=10.1007/BF02196600 }}</ref>

This variant has predictably simple solutions.

A second, more involved variant is
: <math>f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} [100 (x_{i+1} - x_i^2 )^2 + (1-x_i)^2] \quad \mbox{where} \quad \mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_N) \in \mathbb{R}^N.</math><ref>{{cite web |url = http://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-0.14.0/reference/tutorial/optimize.html#unconstrained-minimization-of-multivariate-scalar-functions-minimize|title = Generalized Rosenbrock's function|access-date = 2008-09-16}}</ref>

has exactly one minimum for <math>N=3</math> (at <math>(1, 1, 1)</math>) and exactly two minima for <math>4 \le N \le 7</math> — the global minimum at <math>(1, 1, ..., 1)</math> and a local minimum near <math>\hat{\mathbf{x}} = (-1, 1, \dots, 1)</math>.  This result is obtained by setting the gradient of the function equal to zero, noticing that the resulting equation is a [[rational function]] of <math>x</math>.  For small <math>N</math> the [[polynomial]]s can be determined exactly and [[Sturm's theorem]] can be used to determine the number of [[real number|real]] [[root of a polynomial|roots]], while the roots can be [[Fundamental theorem of algebra#Bounds on the zeroes of a polynomial|bounded]] in the region of <math>|x_i| < 2.4</math>.<ref name="kok2009">{{cite journal |first=Schalk |last=Kok |first2=Carl |last2=Sandrock |title=Locating and Characterizing the Stationary Points of the Extended Rosenbrock Function |journal=Evolutionary Computation |volume=17 |issue= 3|pages=437–53 |year=2009 |doi=10.1162/evco.2009.17.3.437 |pmid=19708775 |hdl=2263/13845 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>  For larger <math>N</math> this method breaks down due to the size of the coefficients involved.

==Stationary points==

Many of the stationary points of the function exhibit a regular pattern when plotted.<ref name="kok2009"/>  This structure can be exploited to locate them.
[[Image:Rosenbrock roots exhibiting hump structures.pdf|thumb|right|300 px|Rosenbrock roots exhibiting hump structures]]

==Optimization examples==
[[File:Rosenbrock.png|thumb|left|200px]]

[[File:Nelder-Mead Rosenbrock.gif|thumb|200px|text-top|left|alt=Rosenbrock function Nelder-Mead|Nelder-Mead method applied to the Rosenbrock function]]

The Rosenbrock function can be efficiently optimized by adapting appropriate coordinate system without using any [[gradient descent|gradient information]] and without building local approximation models (in contrast to many derivate-free optimizers). The following figure illustrates an example of 2-dimensional Rosenbrock function optimization by
[[adaptive coordinate descent]] from starting point <math>x_0=(-3,-4)</math>. The solution with the function value <math>10^{-10}</math> can be found after 325 function evaluations.

Using the [[Nelder–Mead method]] from starting point <math>x_0=(-1,1)</math> with a regular initial simplex a minimum is found with function value <math>1.36 \cdot 10^{-10}</math> after 185 function evaluations. The figure below visualizes the evolution of the algorithm.

{{clear}}

== Use in other fields ==
The Rosenbrock function can be used to create "banana"-shaped distributions, which are a popular benchmark model in statistics and machine learning.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pagani |first=Filippo |last2=Wiegand |first2=Martin |last3=Nadarajah |first3=Saralees |date=2022 |title=An n-dimensional Rosenbrock distribution for Markov chain Monte Carlo testing |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/sjos.12532 |journal=Scandinavian Journal of Statistics |language=en |volume=49 |issue=2 |pages=657–680 |doi=10.1111/sjos.12532 |issn=1467-9469|doi-access=free }}</ref>
